The Otian Standard

How we intend to behave.

This says nothing about what we sell. It is the answer to a different question, written down while it was easy to answer, so that we already know what we decided on the day it gets expensive.

This is the public half of a longer document we keep internally. Version 3.0, 2026. If a line here is one we would not actually hold ourselves to, it should be deleted rather than admired.

What we are actually in

A service business that ships software.

The code is how the service gets delivered. It is not the product. A software company measures features shipped; a service company measures whether one particular person is better off tonight than they were this morning. When those point in different directions we are the second kind, and that decides what we build, what we refuse, and what we apologise for.

What we are trying to do, stated plainly enough to be measured against: give ordinary people an AI agent they actually own, one that takes friction out of the day and puts real time and real control back in their hands.

What we trade away

Said in advance, so it is not decided on a bad month.

Speed of growth, for quality of service

We would rather have a hundred people who would argue with a stranger on our behalf than a thousand who are indifferent. We will turn business away to stay inside what we can actually serve.

Margin, for trust

There is a maximum markup on anything we resell or pass through. It is written down internally and we do not raise it because we discover we could. Growth comes from serving more people, not from taking more per person.

Short-term revenue, for a reputation that compounds

Most of what is on this page costs money in the month it is applied. If we are ever tempted by “just this once, for cash flow”, this line is the answer.

What is not for sale at any price

The privacy architecture, the honesty, and the service standard. We would rather stay small permanently than trade one of them.

The promises

What you should be able to hold us to.

We render more than we are paid for, and we do not mention it.

Every engagement ships at least one thing you did not pay for and did not ask for, chosen because we noticed you needed it. A skill configured you never mentioned, an annoyance fixed while we were in there, a cheat sheet in your own words. We do not invoice it or point at it. If we cannot find one, we did not look closely enough.

We only make money after you are better off.

Before we charge for something we can name what you get: hours back, a task you stop doing, money saved. We will tell you on a call that you are not a fit, that a free tool would serve you better, or that you could do this yourself in an hour. Those are all acceptable answers and none of them costs you anything.

We say the true thing, especially when it costs us.

We describe what the product does today, not next quarter. Limitations sit next to capabilities, in the marketing copy, not buried in an FAQ. Our prices are published so nobody books a call to learn a number. We will not let you stay wrong about what you are buying because correcting you would be awkward.

No dark patterns, no urgency, no surprises.

Cancelling is as easy as starting. No countdown timers for discounts that are not expiring, no pre-checked boxes, no retention gauntlet. No silent renewals and no price rise without hearing it from us first. We will not use urgency, shame or fear to close a sale, and we will not design any flow that works only if you are not reading carefully.

Privacy is the architecture, not a setting.

Archie runs on your computer, on your own AI account, so your conversations go straight to the AI company and never through us. We do not sell, rent, broker or trade your data, aggregated or otherwise, and we do not train on it. If we are ever acquired or wound down, those commitments bind whoever succeeds us or the deal does not happen: that is a term of our agreement, not an intention. The Trust page lists everything we hold, and how to verify it yourself.

You hear back the same day.

Every message gets a real human response the day it arrives, even when the response is “I have read this, I am working on it, you will have a full answer Thursday”. Nobody should wonder whether we saw it. We do not measure our support by call length or tickets closed, because every one of those quietly instructs the person to get off the phone.

When we get it wrong, you hear it from us first.

We tell you before you discover it. We say what happened in plain words, not passive voice: we made a mistake, not an error occurred. We say what we are doing and by when, we make it right materially rather than with an apology, and then we do one more thing. No non-disparagement clause attached to a refund, ever: if you had a bad time you are free to say so.

If it needs a terminal, we have not finished it.

Powerful AI tooling is currently reserved for people who can code, and that is the whole reason we exist. Plain language everywhere. Any jargon that must appear gets explained where it appears. You should always be able to answer three questions: what is it doing, why, and how do I stop it. We assume you are capable and new, never that you will not keep up.

We beat competitors by being better.

Never by misrepresenting them. Every claim we print about another company is sourced to that company’s own page and dated, and our comparison pages carry a section where the alternative wins.

When it is close

The tie-breaker.

When a decision is genuinely close and the promises above point different ways, we run these in order, and if any fails we do not do it. Would we be comfortable if you knew everything we know about this decision, including why we made it? Would we recommend it to a parent, or to a friend who trusted us and would not check? Does it give you more than you paid for, or less? If someone with no loyalty to any of this optimised it ruthlessly, would you still be well served? If it appeared on the front page in two years, would we defend it or explain it away?

If we find ourselves building an argument for why this particular case is an exception, that argument is the signal to stop. The short version, when there is no time for any of it: the money is never the reason.

Anyone can invoke this.

A customer, a developer building for the marketplace, a contractor, or anyone we ever hire can point at a line here and tell us we are not living up to it. That is not an inconvenience. That is the document working.

Tell Us We Fell Short Check the Privacy Claims →

We revise this every year and keep every version, so the changes are visible. If we ever change a promise because it became expensive, we will say so in those words rather than quietly softening it and calling it an update.
